newsitem.title: USA: Lawmakers showered with appeals on de minimis rule.
newsitem.headline: Lawmakers showered with appeals on de minimis rule.

text.p: U.S. lawmakers got an earful this week from state and local officials nationwide opposed to a scale-back of the two-percent de minimis rule.

Letters from officials in Harris County, Texas; the state of Delaware; New York City and other states and localities hit Capitol Hill as a select group of House and Senate members on Friday launched final talks on a tax bill.

The House had voted last month to cut back the de minimis exemption for corporate holdings of munis to a flat $1 million, which lobbyists said would wipe out the provision's value for the muni market.
The Senate did not address the issue in its bill.

"More than 25 percent of the bonds that Harris County issues are owned by corporate investors," County Judge Robert Eckels told Rep. Bill Archer, R-Texas, chair of the House Ways and Means Commmittee, in a letter.

"If this provision is included in the final bill, the future of the bonds we issue would be dramatically, negatively affected because corporations would be discouraged from investing in our bonds," said Eckels, vice president of the National Council of Elected County Executives.
"The burden that Harris County would bear in higher interest payments would be massive," Eckels said.
"We will face higher interest rates on any future new money issues, and immediately on the $450 million in short-term variable rate municipal bonds that we currently have outstanding," Eckels said.
Janet Rzewnicki, Delaware State Treasurer, told Sen. William Roth, chairman of the Senate Finance Committee, that de minimis repeal would be "acutely felt" by her state.

"While non-financial corporations hold only about five percent of outstanding tax-exempt bonds, they play an absolutely vital role in three important market segments: short-term municipal notes, state and local government housing and student loan bonds, and muni leasing transactions," Rzewnicki said.
Barbara Udell, president of the New York City Housing Development Corporation, also raised concerns.

"As an issuer of housing bonds, we are particularly concerned that elimnination of the two percent rule would cause Fannie Mae, which has been a major purchaser of New York City Housing Development Corporation's obligations on a private placement basis, to leave the tax-exempt market," Udell said.
She said Fannie Mae has purchased over $170 million of corporation bonds. The private placements have saved the group nearly $2 million in bond issuance costs, she said.
